relevant_cases.case_summary:
The case originated from a tender invited by the Border Road Organisation (BRO) on 23.02.2023 for the design and construction of twin tunnels, estimated at Rs. 15,04,64,00,000/-. The Appellant, M/s ABCI Infrastructures Pvt Ltd, submitted a bid, but due to what they claimed was a system or typographical error, quoted Rs. 1,569/- instead of Rs. 1,569 crores. Upon discovery of this 'patent error' on 24.08.2023, the Appellant promptly informed BRO the next day, requesting withdrawal from the tender and return of their bid security of Rs. 15,04,64,000/-. BRO, however, adopted an 'obdurate and overly legalistic stance', insisting on the bid, asking for justification, and eventually declaring the Appellant a defaulter, leading to the forfeiture of the bank guarantee. The Appellant's writ petition before the High Court of Himachal Pradesh was dismissed.

The Supreme Court analyzed the principles of mistake in contracts, citing Section 20 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, and precedents regarding equitable relief for material mistakes in bids, especially when promptly notified. The Court found the Appellant's mistake to be 'bald-faced' and a 'patent error' that BRO should have recognized. It criticized BRO's insistence on accepting the unrealistic bid and its subsequent actions as disproportionate. While acknowledging the Appellant's fault in making the error, the Court held that BRO's actions caused unnecessary delay and were not justified. The Court applied the doctrine of proportionality, concluding that BRO's decision to forfeit the entire bank guarantee was excessive given the obvious nature of the mistake.

Ultimately, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's judgment. It directed the Appellant to pay Rs. 1 crore to BRO as a consequence of their error, and in return, ordered BRO to return the Appellant's original bank guarantee of Rs. 15.04 crores within one week of receiving the payment. The Court emphasized the need for a pragmatic approach in such situations.
relevant_cases.winning_arguments: The court largely accepted the petitioner's argument that a patent and obvious mistake occurred in the bid, and that the respondent's actions of insisting on the erroneous bid and forfeiting the bank guarantee were disproportionate and overly legalistic, causing unnecessary delays.

outcome.relief_granted: The Appellant is directed to pay Rs. 1 crore to BRO. Upon receiving this payment, BRO shall return the Appellant's original bank guarantee or demand draft of Rs. 15.04 crores within one week.

relevant_cases.case_summary:
This civil appeal arises from a dispute between Som Datt Builders-NCC-NEC (JV) (appellant) and National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) (respondent) concerning a road construction contract. The core issue was the payment rate for an increased quantity of geogrid, a sub-item in the Bill of Quantities (BOQ). The appellant argued that NHAI's initial estimate for geogrid was erroneous, leading to an increase in actual quantity, and therefore the BOQ rate should apply. NHAI contended that the increase constituted a 'variation' under the contract, allowing for rate renegotiation.

The Dispute Review Board (DRB) and subsequently an Arbitral Tribunal (both composed of technical experts) ruled in favor of the appellant, holding that the quantity increase was not an 'instructed variation' under Clause 51.1 of the contract, and thus the BOQ rate was applicable. The learned Single Judge of the High Court upheld this arbitral award, dismissing NHAI's application under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.

However, a Division Bench of the High Court overturned the Single Judge's decision and the arbitral award, interpreting 'variation' broadly to include automatic quantity increases and deeming the Arbitral Tribunal's interpretation 'unreasonable' and 'opposed to public policy.'

The Supreme Court, in this appeal, found that the Division Bench exceeded its limited jurisdiction under Section 37 of the 1996 Act. The Court affirmed that the interpretation of contract clauses by technical experts (DRB and Arbitral Tribunal), upheld by the Single Judge, was plausible and correct. It reiterated the highly circumscribed nature of judicial interference with arbitral awards, especially when based on a plausible contract interpretation. The Supreme Court concluded that the increase in quantity was not an instructed variation, and the BOQ rate should apply.
relevant_cases.winning_arguments: The Supreme Court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the increase in quantity was not an 'instructed variation' under the contract, and therefore the BOQ rate was applicable. The Court also agreed with the petitioner that the Division Bench exceeded its limited jurisdiction under Section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, by overturning a plausible interpretation of the contract by technical experts and the Single Judge.

outcome.relief_granted: The judgment and order dated 17.11.2009 passed by the Division Bench of the High Court is hereby set aside and the arbitral award dated 03.06.2005 is restored.

relevant_cases.case_summary: Lifecare Innovations Pvt. Ltd., a Micro Enterprise manufacturing a specialized drug, challenged its disqualification from public procurement due to mandatory minimum turnover clauses in tenders. The petitioner argued these clauses were arbitrary, violated Articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution, and contravened the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006 (MSMED Act) and the Public Procurement Policy for Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs) Order 2012, which mandates 25% procurement from MSEs. The respondent, Union of India, contended that the policy was complied with and tender conditions were contractual, allowing the government to assess supplier capability. The Supreme Court held that the Procurement Order 2012 has the force of law, creating statutory duties for authorities, though not an individual 'right' for MSEs. The Court emphasized that judicial review should ensure the effective functioning of these bodies. Consequently, the writ petition was disposed of with directions for the Review Committee and Grievance Cell to examine the interplay of mandatory procurement targets and reserved items, and to examine and set limits for minimum turnover clauses, issuing policy guidelines within 60 days.
relevant_cases.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's underlying concerns regarding the impact of minimum turnover clauses on MSEs and the need for statutory bodies to effectively implement the Procurement Order 2012. It directed the Review Committee and Grievance Cell to address these issues, implying that the petitioner's arguments highlighted a valid systemic problem requiring resolution by the designated authorities.

outcome.relief_granted: The Review Committee and Grievance Cell are directed to examine the issue of mandatory procurement of 25% of goods and services from MSEs in the context of reserved items, and to examine and declare limits of minimum turnover clauses, issuing appropriate policy guidelines within 60 days.

relevant_acts.description: The main purpose of this Act is to establish the National Tax Tribunal for the adjudication of disputes related to direct taxes (levy, assessment, collection, enforcement) and indirect taxes (customs, central excise duties, service tax). It aims to provide a specialized forum for tax-related disputes and to transfer pending cases from High Courts to this Tribunal.

relevant_acts.offences_and_penalties: The National Tax Tribunal has the power to punish for contempt of itself, similar to a High Court, under the provisions of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 (Section 21). The Chairperson, Members, and other officers and employees of the Tribunal are deemed public servants under the Indian Penal Code (Section 25).

# Legal Report: Challenge to Government Tender Process

## Executive Summary
Our client, a construction company, was disqualified from a government tender for a large infrastructure project (valued over INR 500 crores) on a minor technicality, despite being the L-1 bidder in a recent Supreme Court case. We suspect undue preference was given to the winning bidder, and the process was arbitrary, violating principles of natural justice. This report outlines the legal principles relevant to challenging tender processes and arbitrary disqualifications, drawing upon recent Supreme Court judgments. We recommend filing a writ petition in the High Court to seek a fair re-evaluation of bids and challenge the tender award, emphasizing the need for proportionality and adherence to principles of natural justice in government contracting.

## Relevant Legal Principles

### Judicial Review in Contractual Matters
The Supreme Court has consistently held that while courts must exercise restraint in reviewing contractual/commercial matters, the doctrine of proportionality applies when errors are patent and equity merits relief. Intervention is permissible if the tendering authority's action is found to be malicious or a misuse of statutory powers, or if tender conditions violate constitutional rights like Article 14 or 19 [2], [4]. The court's role is to ensure that the tendering authority acts reasonably, fairly, and in the public interest [4].

OF 2025 (Arising out of Special Leave Petition (Civil) No. 25394 of 2023) M/S. ABCI INFRASTRUCTURES PVT. LTD. ..... APPELLANT VERSUS UNION OF INDIA AND OTHERS ..... RESPONDENTS JUDGMENT SANJIV KHANNA, CJI. Leave granted. 2. This is an avoidable litigation. No doubt, there was a mistake on the part of the Appellant € M/s ABCI Infrastructure Private Limited, albeit, instead of taking a pragmatic approach, Respondent No. 2 - Border Road Organisation1 under the Ministry of Defence, Union of India, adopted an obdurate and overly legalistic stance, causing a delay in the project's execution. 3. We begin by briefly discussing the facts of the case: o On 23.02.2023, BRO invited bids for the design and construction of two-lane twin tunnels, approximately 4.1 kilometres long, at Shinkun La Pass, including civil, electrical, and mechanical work, with approaches connecting the Darcha-Padam Highway to NHDL specifications in Himachal Pradesh and Ladakh. The estimated cost of the project was Rs.15,04,64,00,000/- (Rs. 1,504.64 crores). The project was to be completed within 48 months. The bid security amount was Rs.15,04,64,000/- (Rs. M/S Abci Infrastructures Pvt Ltd vs Union Of India on 14 February, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/121916800/ 1 15.04 crores) o Ten bidders, including the Appellant, had submitted their online Technical and Financial Bids on 03.06.2023. The Appellant, like others, had furnished a bank guarantee of Rs.15,04,64,000/-. o On 05.06.2023, technical bids were opened and seven bidders, including the Appellant, were declared technically qualified. o On 24.08.2023, the financial bids of seven bidders, including the Appellant, were opened and the results were declared. 1 Hereinafter, □BRO.‚ o The Appellant was ranked as L-1 bidder, with the bid price of Rs.1,569/- (Rupees One thousand five hundred and sixty-nine only). According to the Appellant, they had quoted a bid price of Rs.1,569 crores. However, due to what they claim was a system error, the quoted amount appeared as just Rs.1,569. o The Appellant claims that they discovered the mistake on 24.08.2023 when the financial bids were opened and announced, and therefore, on the next day, 25.08.2023, they informed the authorities that their actual bid was Rs.1,569 crores, not Rs.1,569. They attributed the error to a typographical mistake or a critical technical issue with the server. While we would not accept the plea of system error, the figure quoted was clearly unrealistic, a patent error and a mistake given the scale and nature of the work tendered. Though the mistake was bald-faced, what followed is incomprehensible, with BRO, insisting on accepting the bid, in spite of letters from the Appellant wanting to withdraw from the tender.

The decision in West Bengal State Electricity Board (supra) was referred to and followed where a relief to the bidder was apparent before this Court in M/s Omsairam Steels & Alloys Pvt. Ltd. v. Director of Mines and Geology, BBSR & Ors.7 This decision observes that while the Court must exercise a lot of restraint in exercising the power of judicial review in contractual commercial matters, the doctrine of proportionality nevertheless applies when the error or mistake is writ large and equity merits the grant of some relief.

A mistake may be unilateral or mutual, but it is always unintentional. If it is intentional, it ceases to be a mistake. Mistakes or errors, though avoidable, are committed inadvertently. They have varied consequences in law. As per Section 20 of the Indian Contract Act, 18722 whereby both M/S Abci Infrastructures Pvt Ltd vs Union Of India on 14 February, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/121916800/ 2 parties to an agreement are under a mistake as to matter of fact essential to an agreement, the agreement is void. The explanation to Section 20 says that an erroneous opinion as to the value of the thing which forms the subject matter of an agreement is not deemed to be a mistake as a matter of fact. This will not be a case covered by Section 20 of the Contract Act. However, this is not the first time that this question has arisen either before this Court or Courts outside of India. In West Bengal State Electricity Board v. Patel Engineering Company Limited and Others3, this Court referred to paragraph 84 of American Jurisprudence (2nd Edition, Volume 64 at page 944), which reads: □As a general rule, equitable relief will be granted to a bidder for a public contract where he has made a material mistake of fact in the bid which he submitted, and where, upon the discovery of that mistake, he acts promptly in informing the public authorities and requesting withdrawal 2 Hereinafter, □Contract Act.‚ 3 (2001) 2 SCC 451. of his bid or opportunity to rectify his mistake particularly when he does so before any formal contract is entered into.‚

31. On the broader issue as to whether □minimum turnover clauses‚ could be violative of Articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution, it is to be seen that the two most relevant criteria for framing suitable conditions in NIT relate to the □capacity‚ and □capability‚ of the bidder. In Association of Registration Plates v. Union of India,24 this Court had an occasion to examine a tender clause which read, ƒThe tenderers/bidders of the joint-venture partners together must have had a minimum annual turnover equivalent to INR 30 crores in the immediately preceding last year. At least 25% of this turnover must be from the licence plate business.
